title: Naskh
def: Abrogation: the replacing of one ruling by a later one, as God wills.
what: The Quran says that whatever verse God abrogates or causes to be forgotten, He brings one better or similar (2:106). Muslims point to clear cases: the prayer direction changed from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:142–150), and the prohibition of wine came in stages (4:43, then 5:90–91).

The term is mainly about rulings of law. Later scholars cut the number of cases drastically: al-Suyuti kept about twenty, and Shah Waliullah five. Some, such as Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, denied abrogation within the Quran altogether.
misread: That Muhammad cancelled the peaceful verses with violent ones, so Islam is violent.
sources: Some early exegetes made sweeping claims that one verse cancelled many. Many scholars rejected this, and the principles the Quran repeats are not treated as cancelled: no compulsion in religion (2:256), kindness and justice to those who have not fought you over your religion (60:8), and the command to deal fairly even with those one dislikes (5:8).

title: Nation of Islam
def: An American movement founded in the 1930s whose beliefs, including that a man was God in person, are not accepted by mainstream Muslims.
what: Wallace D. Fard Muhammad began teaching in Detroit in 1930, and Elijah Muhammad (1897–1975) led the movement from 1934 until his death. Its teachings on race and on Fard’s divinity differ from Islam, which holds that God is one and that Muhammad was the last prophet. Malcolm X left it in 1964, made the pilgrimage, and spoke of seeing Muslims of every colour praying together.
sources: In 1975 Elijah Muhammad’s son, Warith Deen Mohammed, led most followers into mainstream Sunni Islam. Louis Farrakhan revived the Nation in 1978. The Five Percent Nation was founded in Harlem in 1964 by Clarence 13X, who had been a Nation member, and it has its own teachings.

title: No compulsion in religion
def: “There is no compulsion in religion” (2:256): faith cannot be forced.
what: “There is no compulsion in religion; right guidance has become clear from error” (2:256). “If your Lord had willed, all who are on earth would have believed. Would you then compel people to be believers?” (10:99). “Say: the truth is from your Lord; so let whoever wishes believe, and whoever wishes disbelieve” (18:29). Commentators relate 2:256 to Ansari parents who had raised their sons as Jews and wanted to make them Muslims (Abu Dawud).
misread: That the verse was cancelled by the verses on fighting.
sources: A few commentators said 2:256 was abrogated by 9:5 or 9:73, but most hold that it stands, as a general principle that no one may be forced to believe, and as an assertion that faith done under compulsion is without worth. The Prophet’s own constitution at Medina left the Jews their religion (Ibn Ishaq).

title: Noah
def: Noah, the prophet who called his people for 950 years and was saved from the flood in the ark.
what: Chapter 71 is named for him. He called his people night and day (71:5–9), and God told him to build an ark (11:37–38). He stayed among them “a thousand years less fifty” (29:14). When the flood came he saved a pair of every kind (11:40). His son refused to board and drowned (11:42–43). The ark came to rest on al-Judi (11:44).
sources: The Quran presents the flood as a punishment for a people who rejected a prophet, and does not say it covered the whole earth, though many commentators took it so. Noah is among the five greatest messengers, and Muslims give him their salutation of peace (37:79).
